fert.apply1: Phosphorus and potassium are usually applied as a basal dose at sowing or planting; nitrogen is usually split into basal and top-dressing parts.
fert.apply2: Place fertilizer in the soil near the root zone and cover it. Avoid spreading it on leaves, on standing water or just before heavy rain.
fert.apply3: A light irrigation after top-dressing helps uptake (but not in waterlogged fields).
fert.no_qty: No quantities are given on purpose. Use the crop-wise dose from your Soil Health Card or state agriculture department.
fert.note.acidic: Acidic soil (pH below 6.5): organic matter helps and liming may be needed. Apply lime only on soil-test and local advice.
fert.note.alkaline: Alkaline soil (pH above 7.5): add organic matter, and use amendments such as gypsum only if recommended after a soil test.
fert.note.follow_card: Use the crop-wise dose on your Soil Health Card or from your state agriculture department.
fert.note.legume: Groundnut and chickpea fix their own nitrogen, so nitrogen fertilizer is usually not the priority; phosphorus and sulphur often matter more.
fert.note.no_deficiency: No nutrient is rated low. Maintain fertility with organic matter and balanced, soil-test based nutrition.
fert.note.potato: Potato is sensitive to chloride, so sulphate of potash is often preferred over muriate of potash where potassium is needed.
fert.note.rice: In flooded rice, nitrogen is easily lost. Apply it in parts, as advised locally, rather than all at once.
fert.placeholder: Your nutrient status and fertilizer guidance will appear here.
fert.pre1: Do not apply more than recommended: excess fertilizer can harm crops, soil and water.
fert.pre2: Read and follow the product label and your agriculture department's advice.
fert.pre3: Wear gloves and a mask when handling fertilizers, and wash your hands afterwards.
fert.pre4: Store fertilizers dry and away from children, animals, food and seeds.
fert.pre5: Do not mix different products unless the label or an expert says it is safe.
fert.ratings_src: Soil Health Card ratings for available N, P and K (kg/ha). pH: below 6.5 acidic, 6.5 to 7.5 neutral, above 7.5 alkaline (approximate).
fert.sub: Enter your soil-test values to see nutrient status, suitable fertilizer types and precautions.
fert.units_note: Enter values as printed on your Soil Health Card: available N, P and K in kg per hectare, and pH. Ratings follow the Soil Health Card standard. Quantities are not given: use the dose on your card or from your agriculture department.

irr.msg.monitor: Moisture is near the limit or rain is a factor. Check again soon before irrigating.
irr.msg.not_required: Soil moisture is sufficient. You can hold off irrigation.
irr.msg.required: Soil moisture is low for this crop. Irrigation is advisable.
irr.no_control: This tool only gives advice. It does not switch any pump or valve; automatic control would need your own hardware and wiring.

irr.sub: Enter your field conditions to see whether irrigation is needed.
irr.sug.clay: Clay and black soils hold water longer: irrigate less often and avoid overwatering.
irr.sug.drip: Drip irrigation can save water and keep leaves dry for this crop.
irr.sug.heat: Very hot weather increases water loss: watch the crop for wilting.
irr.sug.mulch: Mulching (straw or crop residue) reduces evaporation and helps hold soil moisture.
irr.sug.no_midday: Avoid irrigating in the hottest part of the day; most water is lost to evaporation.
irr.sug.no_waterlog: Avoid waterlogging: standing water for long can damage roots and encourage disease. Keep drainage open.
irr.sug.rain_forecast: Rain is forecast soon (a forecast, not a guarantee): consider waiting before irrigating.
irr.sug.recent_rain: Recent rain was recorded: count it before irrigating.
irr.sug.rice: Rice usually needs a shallow standing water layer during most growth stages; follow local water-saving practices.
irr.sug.sandy: Sandy soil dries quickly: light, more frequent irrigations usually suit it better.
irr.timing.early_morning_evening: Early morning or evening (avoid midday heat)
